Unnecessary quantum criticality in S​U​(3)SU(3) kagome magnets

Yunchao Zhang Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge MA 02139-4307, USA    Xue-Yang Song Affiliation: Department of Physics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Clear Water Bay, Hong Kong, China    T. Senthil Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge MA 02139-4307, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Algebraic/Dirac spin liquids (DSLs) are a class of critical quantum ground states that do not have a quasi-particle description. DSLs and related spin liquid phases often arise in strongly frustrated quantum spin systems, in which strong correlations and quantum fluctuations among constituent spins persist down to zero temperature. In this work, we analyze Mott insulating phases of S​U​(3)SU(3) fermions on a kagome lattice which may realize a DSL phase, described at low energies by (2+1)​d(2+1)d quantum electrodynamics (QED3) with Nf=6N_{f}=6 Dirac fermions. By analyzing the action of physical symmetries on the operators of the QED3 theory, we conclude that the low energy DSL is a quantum critical point that can be accessed by tuning a single microscopic parameter. Aided by the emergent symmetry and anomalies of the low energy effective theory, we conjecture and present supporting arguments that the S​U​(3)SU(3) Kagome magnet DSL is an unnecessary quantum critical point, lying completely within a single phase.

I Introduction

Quantum spin liquids are a class of quantum phases of matter that have appealing features from long-range quantum entanglement to the absence of Landau order [5, 11, 50, 64, 91, 15, 37, 62, 35]. These phases host a wide variety of correlated phenomena, including emergence of anyons, fractionalized excitations, and emergent gauge theory.

Gapped spin liquids, many of which possess intrinsic topological order, and certain classes of gapless spin liquids, such as the Kitaev spin liquid with non-interacting Majorana fermions [49], are amenable to a quasiparticle formulation at low energy. However, there are types of quantum spin liquids that admit no quasi-particle description. An example of such a quantum spin liquid is when the infra-red (IR) theory is a conformal field theory (CFT) fixed point at low energy. Perhaps the simplest example is the spin-1/21/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model in one dimension, which is described by the S​U​(2)1SU(2)_{1} CFT [81, 2, 3].

In (2+1)​d(2+1)d, the simplest known example is the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid (DSL) [36, 37, 69, 62, 35, 68], described by coupling NfN_{f} gapless Dirac fermions ψ\psi to an emergent U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field aa,

ℒD​S​L=∑i=1Nfψ¯i​i​D̸a​ψi+14​e2​fμ​ν​fμ​ν,\mathcal{L}_{DSL}=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{f}}\overline{\psi}_{i}i\not{D}_{a}\psi_{i}+\frac{1}{4e^{2}}f_{\mu\nu}f^{\mu\nu}, (1)

where fμ​ν=∂μaν−∂νaμf_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}a_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}a_{\mu}. For sufficiently large NfN_{f} (≥4\geq 4 according to numerical calculations), this theory flows in the IR to a CFT [7]. The existence of an IR CFT for Nf≥4N_{f}\geq 4 is also consistent with bootstrap studies [20, 51, 4, 31, 52]. The most important local operators in this theory are built from monopole operators, which insert qq units of 2​π2\pi U⁡(1)U(1) flux into the system at a spacetime point. At the CFT fixed point, the scaling dimension of the fundamental monopoles (q=1q=1) is given by [27]

Δ1=0.265​Nf−0.0383+𝒪⁡(1/Nf),\Delta_{1}=0.265N_{f}-0.0383+\mathcal{O}(1/N_{f}), (2)

from a 1/Nf1/N_{f} expansion. For the DSL we examine in this work, Nf=6N_{f}=6 and Δ1∼1.55\Delta_{1}\sim 1.55. Therefore, the monopole is a relevant operator and requires special analysis. If the fundamental monopole is allowed by microscopic symmetries, the DSL will be unstable to monopole proliferation. Note that at sufficiently large Nf≳12N_{f}\gtrsim 12, the monopoles will all be irrelevant [14, 27]. Thus the DSL will be a stable [36] quantum spin liquid phase of matter for sufficiently large-NfN_{f}.

A large body of calculations and simulation suggest the DSL to be the ground state for a variety of lattice spin systems [62, 40, 41, 32, 39]. Furthermore, there are many material platforms that have shown evidence [78, 24, 13, 88, 89, 55, 10] for realizing a DSL state. Fundamentally, these platforms are described as electronic Mott insulators where the quantum spin liquid is formed by interactions between localized spin moments in a lattice. Attempts to move beyond this paradigm by generalizing the spin symmetry to S​U​(N)SU(N) in electronic spin systems have been challenging. Such generalizations usually involve pairing spin and orbital degrees of freedom so locally, electrons can carry a representation of S​U​(N)SU(N) for N>2N>2 even, but the resulting quantum spin-orbital liquids are often not fully S​U​(N)SU(N) symmetric. Moreover, spin-orbit coupling can break the individual spin and orbit-space symmetries, although there are special cases in which strong spin-orbit coupling actually leads to enhanced symmetry [87]. However, as noted earlier, the stability of the DSL state and resulting low energy CFT is greatly enhanced for larger NN (in the systems relevant to our study, Nf∝NN_{f}\propto N), motivating the study of S​U​(N)SU(N)-symmetric spin liquids for larger NN.

Concretely, an S​U​(N)SU(N) spin liquid can potentially be realized in ultracold atomic systems by manipulating nuclear spins. Through loading NN-color atoms on optical lattices, one can can simulate S​U​(N)SU(N)-symmetric interactions in a defect-free and fully controllable environment, providing an experimental platform to engineer and probe exotic phases not yet discovered (or maybe even accessible) in real materials hosting electronic systems. More generally, ultracold gases of alkaline-earth-like atoms prepared in the lowest two electronic states can obey S​U​(2​I+1)SU(2I+1) symmetry, where II is the nuclear spin [84, 33, 29, 34, 17, 65]. With atoms such as 87Sr, the nuclear spin is as large as 9/29/2, leading to an S​U​(10)SU(10) symmetric system. Furthermore, by choosing an appropriate initial state and using the fact that the total number of atoms with a given nuclear spin mm is conserved, atoms with large II such as 87Sr can realize the interactions of atoms with lower II, such that an S​U​(N)SU(N) symmetric system for any N≤2​I+1N\leq 2I+1 can be simulated [29].

In this work, we will focus on Mott insulators of an S​U​(3)SU(3) fermion system with one atom per site on the kagome lattice, which can be programmed on a cold atoms platform [63, 43]. To realize S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetric interactions, one can use alkaline-earth-like atoms with nuclear spin I≥1I\geq 1, such as 173Yb(I=5/2)(I=5/2). We will study a Dirac spin liquid that can potentially occur in such a Mott insulator, and ask where it is situated in the phase diagram.

Through analyzing the quantum numbers of relevant monopole operators, we show there is a relevant monopole operator that transforms trivially under all microscopic symmetries. Therefore, this DSL is unstable, as the presence of this monopole will lead to an instability, possibly towards various symmetry breaking orders. However we argue that there is only a single such relevant operator at the QED3 fixed point that is allowed by the microscopic symmetries. Thus this fixed point will appear as a quantum critical point in the phase diagram of the S​U​(3)SU(3) Kagome magnet.

We further argue that the DSL on the kagome lattice is likely an “unnecessary" quantum critical point (QCP) [12]. Unnecessary QCPs describe transitions within a single phase of matter, in contrast to a conventional QCP that describes the phase transition between two different phases upon the tuning of a relevant perturbation. For other examples, see Refs. [12, 42, 60, 70, 90, 61]. In our previous work, we showed that the Dirac spin liquid also plausibly describes an unncessary QCP within the Neel (or valence bond solid) phase of spin-1/21/2 square lattice magnets [90]. Thus the present work adds the S​U​(3)SU(3) Kagome lattice DSL as another example of such unnecessary QCPs.

Our arguments will rely on an analysis of the relation between the microscopic symmetries of the lattice model and the emergent symmetries of the IR continuum field theory. We will analyze the ’t Hooft anomalies of the latter and the constraints they impose on the low energy physics of the perturbed QED3 theory. We will find that the continuum field theory defined by the perturbing the DSL CFT with its single relevant symmetry-allowed operator has an anomaly that precludes it from flowing to a trivial gapped phase. Further, the anomaly even precludes any gapped symmetric phase even allowing for the possibility of topological order, a phenomenon known as symmetry-enforced gaplessness [76]. We conjecture that the endpoint of the renormalization group (RG) flow away from the DSL is a symmetry broken phase. We show that the same such phase will be obtained for either sign of the relevant perturbation, which then establishes that this DSL is an unnecessary critical point.

Our works adds to the growing number of examples of unnecessary quantum critical points which may thus be not an uncommon phenomenon in quantum many body physics.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II we introduce the kagome lattice mean field ansatz and discuss aspects of the U⁡(1)U(1) DSL state, focusing on the low energy effective field theory and the pivotal role of monopole operators in the critical theory. In Sec. III, we will explain the connection between the lattice symmetries and the emergent symmetries of the infrared continuum QED3 theory. Analyzing the embedding of the lattice symmetries into the continuum to constrain transformation properties of the monopole operators, we will conclude the DSL is unstable due to a monopole trivial under all symmetries. The resulting DSL is then not a stable phase, but a quantum critical point. In Sec. IV we calculate the quantum anomalies of the QED3 QCP, both in the absence and presence of monopole proliferation. Through the nature of the anomaly, we argue that the DSL is a unnecessary quantum critical point, tuned by the proliferation of the singlet monopole. This was previously found in the Nf=4N_{f}=4 DSL on the square lattice [90], so we find that unnecessary criticality may be a feature common to critical points described by QED3. We conclude in Sec. V with some discussion and further outlook.

II Candidate DSL on on the kagome lattice

As discussed in the previous section, by externally trapping ultracold alkaline-earth atoms, one can realize S​U​(3)SU(3)-symmetric interactions on the kagome lattice. A model Hamiltonian that describes such systems is given by the 33-flavor Hubbard model [29, 17],

H=−∑⟨𝒓,𝒓′⟩∑α=13(t𝒓​𝒓′c𝒓​α†c𝒓′​α+h.c.)+U∑𝒓(∑α=13n𝒓​α)2.H=-\sum_{\braket{\bm{r},\bm{r}^{\prime}}}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3}(t_{\bm{r}\bm{r}^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{r}\alpha}c_{\bm{r}^{\prime}\alpha}+h.c.)+U\sum_{\bm{r}}\left(\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3}n_{\bm{r}\alpha}\right)^{2}. (3)

where U>0U>0 captures a finite repulsive on-site density-density interaction and α\alpha labels the S​U​(3)SU(3) spin index. The kagome lattice has a three-site unit cell, and we adopt a convention in which the primitive lattice vectors are defined as

𝑹1=2​a​x^,𝑹2,3=2​a​(±x^+3​y^2),\bm{R}_{1}=2a\hat{x},\quad\bm{R}_{2,3}=2a\left(\frac{\pm\hat{x}+\sqrt{3}\hat{y}}{2}\right), (4)

leading to a hexagonal reciprocal lattice with corners at 𝑲=(2​π3​a,0)\bm{K}=\left(\frac{2\pi}{3a},0\right) and 𝑲′=−𝑲\bm{K}^{\prime}=-\bm{K}.

Focusing on 1/31/3 filling, what are the expected phases as we tune UU? In the the free limit U→0U\rightarrow 0, one obtains a simple tight binding model. Taking a uniform hopping amplitude t𝒓​𝒓′=tt_{\bm{r}\bm{r}^{\prime}}=t,

H=−t∑⟨𝒓,𝒓′⟩∑α=13(c𝒓​α†c𝒓′​α+h.c.),H=-t\sum_{\braket{\bm{r},\bm{r}^{\prime}}}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3}(c^{\dagger}_{\bm{r}\alpha}c_{\bm{r}^{\prime}\alpha}+h.c.), (5)

we find a flat upper band and two lower bands that intersect at Dirac points at 𝑲\bm{K} and 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime}. At 1/31/3 filling, the Fermi level then passes right through the Dirac points, yielding a Dirac semimetal state. The tight binding spectrum ϵ⁡(𝒌)\epsilon(\bm{k}) of Eq. (5) is outlined in Appendix A and shown in Figure 1.

As short range interactions are irrelevant at the Dirac semimetal fixed point, we see the Dirac semimetal is a stable phase for weak Hubbard coupling UU.

For sufficiently large UU, the resulting state is a Mott insulator. The large UU limit is described by an S​U​(3)SU(3) antiferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian,

He​f​f∼t2U​∑⟨𝒓,𝒓′⟩P𝒓,𝒓′,H_{eff}\sim\frac{t^{2}}{U}\sum_{\langle\bm{r},\bm{r}^{\prime}\rangle}P_{\bm{r},\bm{r}^{\prime}}, (6)

where P𝒓,𝒓′P_{\bm{r},\bm{r}^{\prime}} permutes the fermions between two nearest neighbor sites 𝒓\bm{r} and 𝒓′\bm{r}^{\prime}. Each site hosts an S​U​(3)SU(3) spin transforming in the fundamental representation 𝟑\mathbf{3}.

Numerical studies [21, 54, 18, 86] support that the ground state will be be a valence bond crystal (VBS)-like state that preserves C3C_{3} and lattice translations, as a single unit cell can realize an S​U​(3)SU(3) singlet state, ⊗3𝟑=𝟏⊕𝟖2⊕𝟏𝟎\otimes^{3}\mathbf{3}=\mathbf{1}\oplus\mathbf{8}^{2}\oplus\mathbf{10}. This ground state of trimers, shown in Figure 2, is a specific case of the more general NN-simplex solid state for S​U​(N)SU(N) antiferromagnets, in which NN-site S​U​(N)SU(N) singlets cover the plaquettes of an NN-partite lattice [9, 34], generalizing the valence bond solid state as that singlets do not populate two-site bonds, but instead NN-site clusters.

As such a trimerized state on the kagome lattice spontaneously breaks inversion symmetry, the resulting ground state manifold is doubly degenerate.

At intermediate U/t∼1U/t\sim 1, the perturbatively obtained antiferromagnetic Hamiltonian is no longer a suitable description of the system as higher order ring-exchange terms become important [56]. The ground state is not well understood. One possibility is that there is a direct Gross-Neveau transition between the Dirac semi-metal and the VBS state driven by opening a fermion bilinear mass gap. Here however, we will explore an alternate possibility in which near the Mott transition, a Dirac spin liquid may appear, and instead of electrons, fractionalized S​U​(3)SU(3) fermionic “spinons” hop on the kagome lattice with zero background flux. This is the state we will study, and to do so, we employ the parton decomposition of S​U​(3)SU(3) spins 𝑺\bm{S} into fermionic spinons 𝒇\bm{f} by writing

𝑺rA=∑α,η=13fr,α†​Tα​ηA​fr,η,\bm{S}_{r}^{A}=\sum_{\alpha,\eta=1}^{3}f_{r,\alpha}^{\dagger}T_{\alpha\eta}^{A}f_{r,\eta}, (7)

where rr is the site index. The fr,α(†)f_{r,\alpha}^{(\dagger)} are second quantized spinon field operators at site rr with S​U​(3)SU(3) flavor α∈{1,2,3}\alpha\in\{1,2,3\}. Note that the ff operators transform as S​U​(3)SU(3) fundamentals, while the TAT^{A} are the matrix representation of the Hermitian S​U​(3)SU(3) generators acting on the fundamental representation, normalized by the condition Tr⁡[TA​TB]=12​δA​B\operatorname{Tr}[T^{A}T^{B}]=\frac{1}{2}\delta^{AB}. AA is an adjoint index, which ranges in {1,2,…,8}\{1,2,\dots,8\}.

In order to reproduce the physical Hilbert space, the relation in Eq. (7) comes with an additional constraint that ∑αfr,α†​fr,α=1\sum_{\alpha}f_{r,\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{r,\alpha}=1. We then perform a mean field decomposition of the Hubbard Hamiltonian, keeping all spinon hopping terms while preserving the constraint only at the expectation value level.

The result is a mean field Hamiltonian of fermionic particles on a kagome lattice at 1/31/3 filling,

H=−t∑⟨𝒓,𝒓′⟩∑α=13(f𝒓​α†f𝒓′​α+h.c.),H=-t\sum_{\braket{\bm{r},\bm{r}^{\prime}}}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3}(f^{\dagger}_{\bm{r}\alpha}f_{\bm{r}^{\prime}\alpha}+h.c.), (8)

or one atom per lattice site. Note in the above, the fermionic ff operators represent the fractionalized S​U​(3)SU(3) spinons, not the physical electrons. Each site hosts three degenerate atomic states (which can be interpreted as spin states, orbitals, etc.) originating from the three fermion flavors. The dispersion is the same as in Eq. (5) and Figure 1.

We observe that the decomposition in Eq. (7) as realized in Eq. (8) has a U⁡(1)U(1) gauge redundancy generated by the constraint ∑αfr,α†​fr,α=1\sum_{\alpha}f_{r,\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{r,\alpha}=1 that maps each fRf_{R} by a site-dependent phase factor, fr→ei​φr​frf_{r}\rightarrow e^{i\varphi_{r}}f_{r}. In order to restore gauge invariance, we will introduce an emergent U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field aμa_{\mu} that will appear in the low energy field theory 11 1 Shortly, we will find it convenient to place the IR continuum field theory on an arbitrary oriented space-time manifold. We will then regard aa as a spinc connection rather than an ordinary U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field..

II.1 Low energy field theory

Performing an expansion of the momentum-space Hamiltonian around the Dirac points, H⁡(±𝑲+𝒒)−H⁡(±𝑲)H(\pm\bm{K}+\bm{q})-H(\pm\bm{K}), and with a suitable redefinition of the fermion fields, we obtain an effective low energy Dirac Hamiltonian

ℋD​i​r​a​c=vF​∫d2​𝒒(2​π)2​ψα​a†​(qx​τ1+qy​τy)​ψα​a.\mathcal{H}_{Dirac}=v_{F}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{q}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\psi_{\alpha a}^{\dagger}(q_{x}\tau^{1}+q_{y}\tau^{y})\psi_{\alpha a}. (9)

The first index labels the S​U​(3)SU(3) spin, the second index labels the Dirac node (±𝑲\pm\bm{K}), and we have made the spinor index implicit.

Focusing on the 66 Dirac nodes near the Fermi energy coming from the 33 spin degrees of freedom and 22 valleys, one can describe the low energy excitations with the effective Lagrangian,

ℒ=ℒQ​E​D3+Δ​ℒ=∑i=16ψ¯i​D̸a​ψi−14​e2​fμ​ν2+Δ​ℒ,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{QED_{3}}+\Delta\mathcal{L}=\sum_{i=1}^{6}\overline{\psi}_{i}\not{D}_{a}\psi_{i}-\frac{1}{4e^{2}}f_{\mu\nu}^{2}+\Delta\mathcal{L}, (10)

where ψ\psi are two component Dirac fermions with flavor index i∈{1,2,…,6}i\in\{1,2,\dots,6\} and (γ0,γ1,γ2)=(−i​τ3,τ2,−τ1)(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})=(-i\tau^{3},\tau^{2},-\tau^{1}) are the gamma matrices in (2+1)​d(2+1)d. The adjoint Dirac fermion is ψ¯α=(ψ†)α​(−i​γ0)\overline{\psi}^{\alpha}=(\psi^{\dagger})^{\alpha}(-i\gamma^{0}). Lastly, we have defined fμ​ν=∂μaν−∂νaμf_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}a_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}a_{\mu} to be the curvature of the emergent U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field aa.

ℒQ​E​D3\mathcal{L}_{QED_{3}} is exactly the Lagrangian for (2+1)​d(2+1)d quantum electrodynamics (QED3) with Nf=6N_{f}=6 Dirac fermions, which includes minimal coupling of the emergent gauge field to the spinons, in addition to a Maxwell term for the gauge field. Δ​ℒ\Delta\mathcal{L} includes additional operators in QED3 that are allowed by the microscopic symmetries of lattice Hamiltonian.

II.2 Monopole operators

As mentioned in the introduction, in the absence of Δ​ℒ\Delta\mathcal{L}, Eq. (1) flows to an interacting CFT fixed point [6, 8, 7, 36, 47, 46, 27]. However, the most relevant operators in the renormalization group sense are the lowest charge monopole operators with scaling dimension [14, 27] Δ1∼1.55+𝒪⁡(1Nf)\Delta_{1}\sim 1.55+\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{N_{f}}) for Nf=6N_{f}=6. The presence of these monopoles is therefore the most important factor affecting the stability and proximate phases of the DSL. To determine if monopoles are allowed in the action, we must determine their quantum numbers, which are constrained by the symmetries of both the infrared (IR) continuum QED3 theory and the ultraviolet (UV) lattice ansatz. Before delving into the action of symmetry on the monopoles, we first review some background on monopole operators in QED.

To begin, the QED3 action in Eq. (1) generally allows for topologically nontrivial configurations of the gauge field. These can be described by local monopole operators ℳq\mathcal{M}_{q}, which insert an integer qq units of 2​π2\pi U⁡(1)U(1) flux into the system at a spacetime point [14]. Identically, monopole operators ℳq†\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}_{q} can be viewed as non-trivial topological configurations of the gauge field aa, which carry charge qq under a global U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry with conserved current equal to the magnetic flux

jμ=12​π​ϵμ​ν​λ​∂νaλ.j^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda}\partial_{\nu}a_{\lambda}. (11)

We denote this flux symmetry by U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}. In the absence of the Dirac fermions and other matter fields, the monopole perturbation will gap out the photon field and confine gauge charges [59]. In the presence of Dirac fermions, the bare monopole operators ℳq†\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}_{q} must be dressed by fermion zero modes in order to be gauge invariant. The monopoles can be viewed as the basic building blocks of QED3, in that other local operators, including fermion billinears ψ¯i​ψj\overline{\psi}_{i}\psi_{j}, can identified with composites of the gauge-invariant monopole operators.

As we are interested in fluctuations around the zero-flux vacuum, we will focus on the fundamental (q=1q=1) monopoles with scaling dimension [14, 27]

Δ1=0.265​Nf−0.0383+𝒪⁡(1/Nf)∼1.55.\Delta_{1}=0.265N_{f}-0.0383+\mathcal{O}(1/N_{f})\sim 1.55. (12)

Monopoles with higher charge have higher scaling dimension and are irrelevant at the QED3 CFT. For our intuitive understanding, it is useful to transition into the large NfN_{f} limit, in which fluctuations of the gauge field are suppressed and the bare monopole operator ℳ1†\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}_{1} creates a uniform 2​π2\pi flux. The properties of monopole operators can then be deduced from a theory of free Dirac fermions in a constant background magnetic flux. By the Atiyah-Singer index theorem, each Dirac cone contributes a single zero-energy mode. Gauge invariance constrains that exactly half of the zero modes must be filled. In the case of Nf=6N_{f}=6 as in Eq. (10), we obtain a total of (63)=20\binom{6}{3}=20 monopoles, each of which has three zero modes occupied. We can represent the gauge invariant monopole operators schematically by

ϵi​j​k​fi†​fj†​fk†​ℳ1†.\epsilon^{ijk}f_{i}^{\dagger}f_{j}^{\dagger}f_{k}^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{1}^{\dagger}. (13)

We have denoted fi†f^{\dagger}_{i} as the creation operator for the zero mode corresponding to the parent Dirac fermion ψi\psi_{i} and ℳ1†\mathcal{M}_{1}^{\dagger} as the bare monopole operator which simply inserts the unit flux without filling any zero mode. Analogously, antimonopole operators, which insert unit −2​π-2\pi flux, can be defined as the Hermitian conjugates of the monopole operators. The zero modes transform under the flavour symmetry that mixes the 66 Dirac fermions, but as they have vanishing angular momentum in the flux background, the zero modes are singlets under all Lorentz transformations. We also remark that in this large NfN_{f} limit, the monopoles are irrelevant.

Note that other operators are potentially allowed in the Nf=6N_{f}=6 theory as long as they transform trivially under the UV symmetries. However, these operators are most likely irrelevant, as shown in 1/Nf1/N_{f} expansions and numerical simulation. The most relevant, both physically and in the RG sense, include couplings of monopoles to fermion billinears and strength two monopoles. The first type of operator is equivalent to exciting a fundamental monopole. At leading order, it involves transitioning a Dirac zero mode f†f^{\dagger} from the n=−1n=-1 Landau level to n=1n=1, and the resulting operator has an irrelevant scaling dimension Δ1+2​2∼4.38>3\Delta_{1}+2\sqrt{2}\sim 4.38>3 from large NfN_{f}.

The strength two monopole can be created by the double insertion of a strength one monopole or, analogous to the case of a 2​π2\pi flux, by dressing a bare 4​π4\pi flux with 66 out of the 1212 Dirac fermion zero modes. In either case, the strength two monopole scaling dimension estimated from large NfN_{f} is Δ2=0.673​Nf−0.194∼3.84\Delta_{2}=0.673N_{f}-0.194\sim 3.84. While the closeness of Δ2\Delta_{2} to 33 suggests that it could be marginal or relevant due to higher order 1/Nf1/N_{f} corrections, recent Monte Carlo calculations [48] estimate Δ2=3.73​(34)\Delta_{2}=3.73(34) for Nf=4N_{f}=4. As these monopoles become more irrelevant with increasing NfN_{f}, these numerics strongly suggest that the strength two monopole in Nf=6N_{f}=6 is irrelevant as well.

III Symmetries of the DSL

In this section, we will illustrate how symmetries of the microscopic theory constrain the allowed monopole operators, following the methods employed in Refs. [73, 72]. While we are only considering a specific lattice ansatz, the methods used illustrate a more general framework. Whenever a lattice model produces as emergent critical field theory in the IR limit, the operators in the IR field theory should be interpreted physically as coarse-grained, dressed lattice operators. The correspondence is made by matching the symmetries of lattice operators with those of the IR field theory. At a more abstract level, there is some embedding/group homomorphism (φ\varphi) of the lattice symmetries GU​VG_{UV} into the symmetry group GI​RG_{IR} of the IR theory,

φ:GU​V→GI​R.\varphi\;:\;G_{UV}\rightarrow G_{IR}. (14)

Our concern will be to find the symmetry action of φ⁡(GU​V)\varphi(G_{UV}) on the fundamental monopole operators to find which are allowed from the UV lattice theory.

III.1 Symmetries of the microscopic system: the group GU​VG_{UV}

From the UV lattice model (which we take to be a spin model with spins transforming in the fundamental representation of S​U​(3)SU(3)), the total microscopic symmetry is

GU​V=P​S​U​(3)s⋊𝒯×Gl​a​t​t​i​c​e,G_{UV}={PSU(3)_{s}}\rtimes\mathcal{T}\times G_{lattice}, (15)

where P​S​U​(N)=S​U​(N)/Z⁡(S​U​(N))PSU(N)=SU(N)/Z(SU(N)) is the projective special unitary group. The point group symmetries of the kagome lattice, Gl​a​t​t​i​c​eG_{lattice}, are generated by translations (T1,2T_{1,2}) along the primitive Bravais lattice vectors 𝑹1,2\bm{R}_{1,2}, rotations (C6C_{6}) by 2​π/62\pi/6 around the origin of a hexagonal plaquette, and a reflection symmetry (ℛy\mathcal{R}_{y}) taking y→−yy\rightarrow-y. Furthermore, we have P​S​U​(3)sPSU(3)_{s} spin rotations and (antiunitary) time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Note that as there are 3 sites per kagome unit cell, and we have S​U​(3)SU(3) spins which can then form a singlet within each unit cell, there is no Lieb-Schultz-Mattis (LSM) constraint coming from just the interplay between lattice translations and the P​S​U​(3)PSU(3) symmetry. Indeed, the construction of the translation-invariant VBS Mott insulator described earlier illustrates the absence of such a non-trivial LSM constraint.

III.2 Symmetries of QED3: the group GI​RG_{IR}

We now review the symmetries of the continuum QED3 theory which form GI​RG_{IR}. The theory ℒQ​E​D3\mathcal{L}_{QED_{3}} from Eq. (1) has a continuous Lorentz group symmetry 22 2 At the fixed point to which the QED3 flows, we will also have conformal symmetry., S​O​(2,1)LSO(2,1)_{L}, and the familiar discrete Lorentz symmetry actions of time reversal 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR}, partial reflection ℛI​R\mathcal{R}_{IR}, and charge conjugation 𝒞I​R\mathcal{C}_{IR}. The IR subscript is a reminder that these bare actions in GI​RG_{IR} are not the same as the corresponding physical symmetry in GU​VG_{UV}. The discrete symmetries can be chosen to act on the Dirac fermions as

𝒯I​R\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{IR}\; :ψ⁡(t,𝒓)→γ1​ψα​(−t,𝒓),i→−i,\displaystyle:\;\psi(t,\bm{r})\rightarrow\gamma^{1}\psi^{\alpha}(-t,\bm{r}),\quad i\rightarrow-i, (16)
ℛI​R\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{IR}\; :ψ⁡(t,𝒓)→−i​γ2​ψα​(t,R​𝒓),\displaystyle:\;\psi(t,\bm{r})\rightarrow-i\gamma^{2}\psi^{\alpha}(t,R\bm{r}), (17)
𝒞I​R\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{IR}\; :ψ⁡(t,𝒓)→(ψ¯α​(t,𝒓)​(i​γ1))T.\displaystyle:\;\psi(t,\bm{r})\rightarrow(\overline{\psi}^{\alpha}(t,\bm{r})(i\gamma^{1}))^{T}. (18)

Note however that the Dirac fermions are not local operators; we will use them as a device to deduce the symmetry action Internally on the Dirac fermions, we also have (what is roughly) a global S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f} flavor symmetry, ψα→Uα​β​ψβ\psi_{\alpha}\rightarrow U_{\alpha\beta}\psi_{\beta} for U∈S​U​(6)fU\in SU(6)_{f}. However we should quotient out by the center of S​U​(6)SU(6) (which can be combined with a gauge transformation) so that the theory naively has an internal symmetry group of P​S​U​(6)=S​U​(6)f/ℤ6PSU(6)=SU(6)_{f}/\mathbb{Z}_{6}. In addition we have a U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} symmetry associated with conservation of the gauge flux d​a/2​πda/2\pi. This symmetry acts trivially on the Dirac fermions. The true internal symmetry group, as we will show below using the monopole operators, is not actually the simple product P​S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​pPSU(6)\times U(1)_{top}, but a quotient group.

As noted earlier, in the presence of a charge one monopole ℳ1†\mathcal{M}_{1}^{\dagger}, each Dirac mode contributes a single fermion zero mode fif_{i}, which behaves as a Lorentz scalar while transforming as ψi\psi_{i} under S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f}. We will denote ϕA\phi_{A} to be the monopole represented by the “wave function”

ϕA†\displaystyle\phi_{A}^{\dagger} =ℱA†​ℳ†,\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}, (19)
ℱA†\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\dagger} =f[A1†fA2†fA3]†,\displaystyle=f_{[A_{1}}^{\dagger}f_{A_{2}}^{\dagger}f_{A_{3}]}^{\dagger},

where for convenience of notation, A=[A1,A2,A3]A=[A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}] denotes an antisymmetrized multi-index defined by

T[a1​…​ap]=1p!​ϵa1​…​ap​ϵb1​…​bp​Tb1​…​bp.T_{[a_{1}\dots a_{p}]}={\frac{1}{p!}}\epsilon_{a_{1}\dots a_{p}}\epsilon^{b_{1}\dots b_{p}}T_{b_{1}\dots b_{p}}. (20)

As the ff’s transform in the fundamental of S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f} and ℳ\mathcal{M} is an S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f} singlet, ϕ†\phi^{\dagger} will transform in the 33-fold antisymmetric tensor product of the S​U​(6)SU(6) fundamental representation, which is the irreducible representation of S​U​(6)SU(6) whose Young tableau has one column and three rows. This representation is self conjugate and symplectic, with an invariant bilinear given by

EA​B=E[A1,…,A3]​[B1,…,B3]=16​ϵA1​…​A3​B1​…​B3=EA​B.E_{AB}=E_{[A_{1},\dots,A_{3}][B_{1},\dots,B_{3}]}=\frac{1}{6}\epsilon_{A_{1}\dots A_{3}B_{1}\dots B_{3}}=E^{AB}. (21)

In the case Nf≡0(mod4)N_{f}\equiv 0\pmod{4} as was considered in previous works, the representation is instead orthogonal, and EA​BE_{AB} is symmetric instead of antisymmetric [16]. In either case, EA​BE_{AB} should be thought of as acting on the space of monopole wave functions ϕA†\phi_{A}^{\dagger}, equivalent to the Nf/2N_{f}/2-fold antisymmetric product on ℂNf\mathbb{C}^{N_{f}}. In summary, we see that the ϕ†\phi^{\dagger} have charge one under the magnetic U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} symmetry, transform in the self-conjugate antisymmetric representation of S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f}, and are Lorentz scalars.

The center of S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f} is made of matrices of the form ωn​𝕀6×6\omega^{n}\mathbb{I}_{6\times 6} for ω=e2​π​i/6\omega=e^{2\pi i/6}, so the true faithful internal symmetry group acting on the monopoles is

GI​R=S​U​(6)f×U​(1)t​o​pℤ6,G_{IR}=\frac{SU(6)_{f}\times U(1)_{top}}{\mathbb{Z}_{6}}, (22)

where ℤ6\mathbb{Z}_{6} is generated by the element (ω​𝕀6×6,−1)∈S​U​(6)f×U​(1)t​o​p(\omega\mathbb{I}_{6\times 6},-1)\in SU(6)_{f}\times U(1)_{top}. The quotient action arises because ω​𝕀∈S​U​(6)f\omega\mathbb{I}\in SU(6)_{f} and a π\pi rotation in U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} are indistinguishable when acting on gauge invariant operators. The full IR symmetry is then GI​RG_{IR} in addition to the Lorentz and discrete symmetries such as time reversal, reflection, and charge conjugation.

To define the action of the discrete, infrared Lorentz symmetries on the monopole operators, we must determine how they act on the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} and S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f} symmetry. First, we observe that for all three discrete actions, U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} charge is reversed, so ϕ\phi is mapped to its Hermitian conjugate. 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR} and ℛI​R\mathcal{R}_{IR} do not interact with the S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f} representation of the monopoles, but 𝒞I​R\mathcal{C}_{IR} changes an S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f} representation to its complex conjugate. Choosing appropriate phases allows us to define

𝒯I​R\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{IR}\; :ϕA†→i​EA​B​ϕB,\displaystyle:\;\phi_{A}^{\dagger}\rightarrow iE_{AB}\phi^{B}, (23)
ℛI​R\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{IR}\; :ϕA†→−EA​B​ϕB,\displaystyle:\;\phi_{A}^{\dagger}\rightarrow-E_{AB}\phi^{B},
𝒞I​R\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{IR}\; :ϕA†→i​ϕB,\displaystyle:\;\phi_{A}^{\dagger}\rightarrow i\phi^{B},

where phases up to a U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} action were chosen so 𝒯I​R2=(𝒞I​R​ℛI​R)2=1\mathcal{T}_{IR}^{2}=(\mathcal{C}_{IR}\mathcal{R}_{IR})^{2}=1 on the monopole operators [16]. These phase ambiguities are a matter of convention.

III.3 Embedding GU​VG_{UV} into GI​RG_{IR}

The parton construction leading to the QED3 theory enables us to deduce how GU​VG_{UV} embeds into GI​RG_{IR}. We begin by noting that as the fermionic spinons are not gauge invariant operators, the microscopic symmetries need not act linearly on them. This is formalized with the notion of the spin liquid’s projective symmetry group [79]. The microscopic symmetries can then be written in terms of elements of the projective symmetry group that transform the physical spin operators 𝑺\bm{S} as desired. However, the projective symmetry group also has a subgroup, termed the invariant gauge group (IGG), that leaves the physical spin operators invariant. Consequently, symmetry actions on the spinons are only defined modulo elements of the IGG. The IGG of our mean field ansatz is exactly the U⁡(1)U(1) gauge group emergent from the parton decomposition. Once the microscopic symmetry actions on the partons are defined, they can be projected down to the IR degrees of freedom, yielding φ⁡(GU​V)\varphi(G_{UV}).

Due to the simplicity of our spin liquid ansatz, the kagome lattice symmetries can be realized linearly on the spinons. The induced symmetry action on the Dirac fermions ψ\psi is listed in Table 1 and shown in Figure 3.

We have defined μ\mu to act on the Dirac node index, τ\tau to act on the Lorentz (spinor) index, and time reversal to include complex conjugation. We see these symmetries forbid all mass terms ψ†​μi​τj​ψ\psi^{\dagger}\mu^{i}\tau^{j}\psi.

We note that the UV time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T} does not act on the S​U​(3)SU(3) orbital index. Knowing the UV symmetry action on the partons, we now determine how GU​VG_{UV} is embedded into GI​RG_{IR}. Note that, as is true in general for the projective symmetry group of spin liquids, the P​S​U​(3)PSU(3) symmetry of the UV lattice ansatz will be embedded as a subgroup of the S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f} flavor symmetry of QED3. Projected onto the IR symmetries, the lattice symmetry elements (as in Table 1) will also clearly include elements of P​S​U​(6)fPSU(6)_{f}, although now possibly supplemented by discrete QED3 symmetry factors. Fortunately, the simplicity of our ansatz allows to decompose

S​U​(6)f→S​U​(3)s×S​U​(2)vSU(6)_{f}\rightarrow SU(3)_{s}\times SU(2)_{v} (24)

as all of the UV spin and lattice symmetries decouple in this manner within S​U​(6)fSU(6)_{f}. Then, within ((S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p))/ℤ6({(SU(6)\times U(1)_{top})})/{\mathbb{Z}_{6}}, the UV symmetry operators that act on the monopoles can be thought of as elements of

P​S​U​(3)s×P​S​U​(2)v×U​(1)t​o​p⊂(S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p)ℤ6.\displaystyle PSU(3)_{s}\times PSU(2)_{v}\times U(1)_{top}\subset\frac{(SU(6)\times U(1)_{top})}{\mathbb{Z}_{6}}. (25)

The P​S​U​(3)PSU(3) symmetry embeds into the IR symmetry (S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p)/ℤ6(SU(6)\times U(1)_{top})/\mathbb{Z}_{6} exactly as induced by the branching in Eq. (24), which factors the S​U​(6)SU(6) flavor symmetry into a part coming from the UV S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetry and an emergent S​U​(2)SU(2) valley symmetry. From the action of the GU​VG_{UV} symmetries (Table 1) on ψ\psi, we can deduce how the lattice symmetries are embedded in

P​S​U​(3)s×P​S​U​(2)v×S​O​(2,1)L.PSU(3)_{s}\times PSU(2)_{v}\times SO(2,1)_{L}. (26)

For example, one can see that T1T_{1} will be embedded as the element 𝕀3×3⊗ei​𝑲⋅𝑹1​μ3⊗𝕀2×2\mathbb{I}_{3\times 3}\otimes e^{i\bm{K}\cdot\bm{R}_{1}\mu^{3}}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{2\times 2}, while an S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetry gg will be embedded as g⊗𝕀2×2⊗𝕀2×2g\otimes\mathbb{I}_{2\times 2}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{2\times 2}. For calculational ease, it is useful to separate the fundamental monopoles into a basis that respects the branching in Eq. (24), and this procedure is outlined in Appendix B.

However, there are two complications we must address. Firstly, the embedding of the lattice symmetries φ⁡(GU​V)\varphi(G_{UV}), into entire IR symmetry group seems unclear, as the action of GU​VG_{UV} on ψ\psi does not completely specify how to incorporate the IR discrete Lorentz symmetries, which from Eq. (23) all act the monopole operators as some combination of Hermitian conjugation and multiplication by the invariant tensor EA​BE_{AB}. In previous works that considered Nf≡0(mod4)N_{f}\equiv 0\pmod{4} [72, 16], EA​BE_{AB} and the other actions of the IR discrete symmetries could be included within the S​U​(N)s×S​U​(M)vSU(N)_{s}\times SU(M)_{v} action. However, for our case where Nf=6N_{f}=6, this is no longer true, and the IR symmetries cannot always simply be absorbed into S​U​(3)s×S​U​(2)vSU(3)_{s}\times SU(2)_{v} as transformations as EA​BE_{AB} does not respect this branching. Instead, the embedding of the lattice symmetries should arise from comparing Eqs. (16) to (18) to the PSG action, as done in [73]. For example, on the monopole operators, lattice time reversal acts as the IR time reversal on the ψ\psi’s composed with a valley rotation μ2\mu^{2}.

The second complication, as noted earlier, is the presence of a phase ambiguity associated with the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} factor. From GU​VG_{UV}, there is no information in the projective symmetry group regarding U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}. Furthermore, the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} factor involves inherently UV physics, as it can be thought of as an effective Berry phase accumulated when the monopoles moves in a lattice charge background. In Appendix C, we use analytic arguments and techniques from band theory as described in [73, 72] to identify to derive the correct U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} Berry phase.

Using those results, we can explicitly write down the embedding φ\varphi that maps the UV symmetry elements into

(S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p)ℤ6\frac{(SU(6)\times U(1)_{top})}{\mathbb{Z}_{6}} (27)

in addition to Lorentz group factors and discrete symmetries. The mapping is as follows:

φ⁡(g∈S​U​(3))\displaystyle\varphi(g\in SU(3)) =(g⊗𝕀2×2v⊗1t​o​p)⊗𝕀2×2L,\displaystyle=(g\otimes\mathbb{I}^{v}_{2\times 2}\otimes 1^{top})\otimes\mathbb{I}^{L}_{2\times 2},
φ⁡(T1,2)\displaystyle\varphi(T_{1,2}) =(𝕀3×3s⊗ei​𝑲⋅𝑹1,2​μ3⊗1t​o​p)⊗𝕀2×2L,\displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{I}^{s}_{3\times 3}\otimes e^{i\bm{K}\cdot\bm{R}_{1,2}\mu^{3}}\otimes 1^{top}\right)\otimes\mathbb{I}^{L}_{2\times 2},
φ⁡(C6)\displaystyle\varphi(C_{6}) =(𝕀3×3s⊗i​μ1⊗1t​o​p)⊗e−i​π6​τ3,\displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{I}^{s}_{3\times 3}\otimes i\mu^{1}\otimes 1^{top}\right)\otimes e^{-\frac{i\pi}{6}\tau^{3}},
φ⁡(ℛy)\displaystyle\varphi(\mathcal{R}_{y}) =(𝕀3×3s⊗i​μ3⊗1t​o​p)⊗𝕀2×2L∘ℛI​R,\displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{I}^{s}_{3\times 3}\otimes i\mu^{3}\otimes 1^{top}\right)\otimes\mathbb{I}_{2\times 2}^{L}\circ\mathcal{R}_{IR},
φ⁡(𝒯)\displaystyle\varphi(\mathcal{T}) =(𝕀3×3s⊗i​μ2⊗i)⊗i​τ2∘𝒯I​R.\displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{I}^{s}_{3\times 3}\otimes i\mu^{2}\otimes i\right)\otimes i\tau^{2}\circ\mathcal{T}_{IR}. (28)

In the above, we have denoted the matrices ⊗𝕄s,v,t​o​p,L\otimes\mathbb{M}^{s,v,top,L} to act on the S​U​(3)sSU(3)_{s}, S​U​(2)vSU(2)_{v}, U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}, and Lorentz group factors, respectively.

From our analysis in Appendices B and C, we find a single trivial monopole

Re⁡(Φ1†+Φ2†)+Im⁡(Φ1†+Φ2†).\operatorname{Re}(\Phi_{1}^{\dagger}+\Phi_{2}^{\dagger})+\operatorname{Im}(\Phi_{1}^{\dagger}+\Phi_{2}^{\dagger}). (29)

As mentioned earlier, we see that the Nf=6N_{f}=6 charge one monopole is a relevant perturbation, leading to the Dirac spin liquid not being a stable gapless phase as the monopole proliferates to confine gauge fluctuations and a fermion mass develops to gap the matter fields. Most likely, there will be an instability towards some proximate symmetry breaking orders. In our case, there are also many symmetry allowed mass-monopole and monopole-monopole billinear couplings, though these are irrelevant due to their large scaling dimension.

Therefore, our analysis supports that the DSL is a quantum critical point, tuned by the proliferation of a single symmetry allowed monopole. We will assume that the UV symmetry allowed operators in the higher representations of S​U​(6)SU(6) are irrelevant. These assumptions, discussed in in Appendix D, are similar to the ones needed for a stable Dirac spin liquid phase for Nf=4N_{f}=4 on the kagome and triangular lattices, and a DSL critical point on the square lattice [31, 90]. In Appendix E, we also comment on the possibility that a chiral mass ψ¯​ψ\overline{\psi}\psi is condensed, which would suppress monopole proliferation. However, this requires spontaneous time reversal symmetry breaking, which we will not consider further.

IV ’t Hooft anomalies of Nf=6N_{f}=6 QED3

In this section, we will focus on the continuum theory and perform a systematic analysis of the quantum anomalies associated with Nf=6N_{f}=6 QED3, Eq. (10), with and without monopoles. The anomalies strongly constrain the IR behavior of the (perturbed) DSL. This has been done in other cases in [72, 16, 38, 25], but our calculation considers the anomaly in the presence of monopole perturbations. Furthermore, the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis-Oshikawa-Hastings (LSMOH) theorems [53, 57, 30] forbid some systems from having a trivially gapped state and can be used in conjunction with the ’t Hooft anomalies in order to restrict the possible values of monopole phases. However, the LSMOH anomalies associated with translation vanish when there are NN fundamental S​U​(N)sSU(N)_{s} spins per unit cell, which is true for our kagome lattice ansatz. However, there is an anomaly between the S​U​(3)sSU(3)_{s} symmetry and rotation (or reflection), which we will derive from the IR anomaly.

The ’t Hooft anomaly of the symmetry GG can be probed by attempting to gauge GG. The action that arises can be interpreted as living on the boundary of a (3+1)​d(3+1)d symmetry protected topological phase on a manifold M4M_{4}, and the anomaly can be detected by dependence of the partition function on the choice of M4M_{4} or the extension of gauge fields to M4M_{4}. We will consider two relevant choices of GG:

  • •

    (S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p)/ℤ6(SU(6)\times U(1)_{top})/\mathbb{Z}_{6}, the internal symmetry of the QED3 fixed point.

  • •

    (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3}, corresponding to the kagome DSL case, in which we have perturbed the CFT with the symmetry-allowed monopole. The quotient ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} is the diagonal center of each S​U​(3)SU(3) factor.

(We will also briefly consider a “mid-IR" theory of Dirac fermions coupled to a U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field with P​S​U​(3)s×P​S​U​(2)v×U​(1)t​o​pPSU(3)_{s}\times PSU(2)_{v}\times U(1)_{top}, relevant to Dirac spin liquids with S​U​(3)SU(3) spin and S​U​(2)SU(2) valley symmetries.) In all cases, we find a nontrivial ’t Hooft anomaly, precluding the existence a trivial, symmetric, gapped ground state. Furthermore, we argue that the form of the anomaly with the monopoles included prohibits a symmetric topologically ordered phase, which is an example of symmetry-enforced gaplessness [76, 77, 71, 75, 23, 22]. Therefore, the only allowed IR theory in the presence of the monopole must be one that is symmetry breaking or, if symmetry preserving, must be gapless.

IV.1 (S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p)/ℤ6(SU(6)\times U(1)_{top})/\mathbb{Z}_{6}

In this section, we will explore the anomalies of QED3 without monopoles, but with the full IR (S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p)/ℤ6(SU(6)\times U(1)_{top})/\mathbb{Z}_{6} symmetry. We will also introduce many tools and methods that will be useful in analyzing the later cases with different symmetry.

It will be convenient to place the continuum theory on an arbitrary closed oriented 3-manifold M3M_{3} with a metric gg and to introduce background gauge fields for the (S​U​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p)/ℤ6(SU(6)\times U(1)_{top})/\mathbb{Z}_{6} global internal symmetry. In the presence of these background gauge fields and metric, the action SS will not be well-defined as a (2+1)​d(2+1)d theory; rather it requires an extension of gg and the background gauge fields (though not the dynamical fields) to a bulk (3+1)​d(3+1)d theory. We can view the action as arising from a (3+1)​d(3+1)d SPT bulk on a manifold M4M_{4} action whose restriction to the boundary M3=∂M4M_{3}=\partial M_{4} yields the exact gauged action for our original Nf=6N_{f}=6 QED3 theory. To characterize the anomaly, it is sufficient to consider the bulk theory on a closed manifold M4M_{4}: the difference in the partition function phase between two choices of an open M4M_{4} could be detected through Sb​u​l​kS_{bulk} evaluated on the closed manifold M~4\tilde{M}_{4}, where M~4\tilde{M}_{4} is obtained by gluing the two choices of M4M_{4} along their boundaries.

We thus turn on background gauge fields 𝒜6\mathcal{A}^{6} for S​U​(6)SU(6) and 𝒜t​o​p\mathcal{A}^{top} for U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}. Due to the ℤ6\mathbb{Z}_{6} quotient, all local operators in the theory transform faithfully under P​S​U​(6)PSU(6), and we will therefore regard 𝒜6\mathcal{A}^{6} as a P​S​U​(6)PSU(6) gauge bundle. Not every such bundle can be lifted to an S​U​(6)SU(6) bundle. The obstruction to doing so is captured by a characteristic class [26, 44, 28], known as the Brauer or Stiefel-Whitney class, w2∈H2​(M4,ℤ6)w_{2}\in H^{2}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{6}).

To ensure that both S​U​(6)SU(6) and U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} have a common quotient by ℤ6\mathbb{Z}_{6}, we also have the cocycle condition

∮12​w2+d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∈ℤ.\oint\frac{1}{2}w_{2}+\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\in\mathbb{Z}. (30)

To see how this arises, note that for each 2​π2\pi strength monopole, there are six zero modes, of which three of them will attach to and dress the bare monopole. Rotating by an element e2​π​i​m6​𝕀e^{\frac{2\pi im}{6}}\mathbb{I} in the ℤ6\mathbb{Z}_{6} center of the flavor S​U​(6)SU(6) contributes to a phase of e2​π​i​m2e^{\frac{2\pi im}{2}}, which can be compensated by a U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} rotation. Therefore, only m(mod2)m\pmod{2} is important and can lead to a fractional flux of At​o​pA_{top}.

In what follows we will construct the QED3 theory by first considering a ‘parent’ theory of Nf=6N_{f}=6 massless Dirac fermions in (2+1)​d(2+1)d and then coupling in the dynamical U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field. The parent Dirac fermion theory has a global U⁡(6)=(U​(1)a×S​U​(6))/ℤ6U(6)=({U(1)_{a}\times SU(6)})/{\mathbb{Z}_{6}} symmetry and we include a coupling to a background U⁡(6)U(6) gauge field. We have denoted the U⁡(1)U(1) factor in U⁡(6)U(6) as U​(1)aU(1)_{a} and the corresponding gauge field will be denoted aa. For now aa is a background gauge field but we will soon promote it to a dynamical gauge field to define the QED3 theory.

In the parent theory, the only fields with unit charge under U​(1)aU(1)_{a} transform in the fundamental of S​U​(6)SU(6) and are fermions (spinors of the tangent bundle of M4M_{4}). Hence we obtain the twisted flux condition

∮16​w2+12​w2T​M+d​a2​π∈ℤ,\oint\frac{1}{6}w_{2}+\frac{1}{2}w_{2}^{TM}+\frac{da}{2\pi}\in\mathbb{Z}, (31)

which ensures that the U⁡(6)U(6) gauge field couples properly to fermions. In the above, we have used w2T​M∈H2​(M4,ℤ2)w_{2}^{TM}\in H^{2}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{2}) to be the Stiefel–Whitney class of the tangent bundle of M4M_{4}. Therefore, in the presence of S​U​(6)SU(6), the U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field aa becomes a generalized form of a spinc connection. Intuitively, this relation captures the twisting of the transition functions that are allowed because in order for the fermions to be well-defined, a particular combination of the gauge bundle transition functions need to satisfy the usual cocyle compatibility condition. More physically, a defect in the cocycle condition of one principal gauge bundle can be compensated for by some nontrivial flux in another bundle.

Now to explicitly derive the action, we will Pauli-Villars regularize the Dirac fermions, where we define the partition function of a Dirac fermion coupled to a general gauge field AA and gravitational metric gg to be

Z​[A,g]P​V=|Z⁡[A,g]|​exp⁡(−i​π2​η​[A,g]).Z[A,g]_{PV}=|Z[A,g]|\exp\left(-\frac{i\pi}{2}\eta[A,g]\right). (32)

Here η⁡[A,g]\eta[A,g] is the η\eta invariant of the Dirac operator [82, 66, 67], which is classically equal to the half-integer level Chern-Simons (CS) term arising from an additional gapped Dirac fermion. To define the Dirac theory, we must extend gg, 𝒜t​o​p\mathcal{A}_{top}, and the U⁡(6)U(6) gauge field 𝒜^​(a,𝒜6)\hat{\mathcal{A}}(a,\mathcal{A}^{6}) into the bulk manifold M4M_{4}. We now write the free Nf=6N_{f}=6 Dirac fermion theory, together with its background gauge fields as

ZD​i​r​a​c=∫[𝒟​ψ]​e−Sb​o​u​n​d​a​r​y​[ψ,a,𝒜6,𝒜t​o​p,g]−Sb​u​l​k​[a,𝒜6,𝒜t​o​p,g].Z_{Dirac}=\int\left[\mathcal{D}\psi\right]e^{-S_{boundary}[\psi,a,\mathcal{A}^{6},\mathcal{A}^{top},g]-S_{bulk}[a,\mathcal{A}^{6},\mathcal{A}^{top},g]}. (33)

From the η\eta invariant, one can find

S=Sb​o​u​n​d​a​r​y+Sb​u​l​k=∫[(ψ¯​D̸[a,𝒜6,𝒜t​o​p,g]​ψ)P​V+i​32​C​S​[a]+i​12​C​S​[𝒜6]+6​i​C​Sg​r​a​v​[g]−i​12​π​a∧d​𝒜t​o​p],S=S_{boundary}+S_{bulk}=\int\left[\left(\overline{\psi}\not{D}_{[a,\mathcal{A}^{6},\mathcal{A}^{top},g]}\psi\right)_{PV}+i\frac{3}{2}CS[a]+i\frac{1}{2}CS[\mathcal{A}^{6}]+6iCS_{grav}[g]-i\frac{1}{2\pi}a\wedge d\mathcal{A}^{top}\right], (34)

where the additional topological terms are introduced to properly preserve time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T} in the presence of the the η\eta invariant. The CS terms are defined by d​C​S​[A]=14​π​Trf​u​n​d​[F∧F]dCS[A]=\frac{1}{4\pi}\operatorname{Tr}_{fund}[F\wedge F] and d​C​S​[g]=1196​π​Trv​e​c​[R∧R]dCS[g]=\frac{1}{196\pi}\operatorname{Tr}_{vec}[R\wedge R], where F=d​A+A∧AF=dA+A\wedge A is the curvature of AA and RR is the Riemann curvature tensor of M4M_{4}.

As discussed earlier, half-integer CS levels are not gauge invariant, so it is important to view them as arising from a (3+1)​d(3+1)d bulk action on a manifold M4M_{4} action whose restriction to the boundary ∂M4\partial M_{4} yields exact gauged action SS in Eq. (34). Using Stokes’ theorem, we can write this bulk action as

Sb​u​l​k2​π​i=32​p1​[a]−38​σ+12​p1​[𝒜6]−∫M4d​a2​π∧d​𝒜t​o​p2​π,\frac{S_{bulk}}{2\pi i}=\frac{3}{2}p_{1}[a]-\frac{3}{8}\sigma+\frac{1}{2}p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]-\int_{M_{4}}\frac{da}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}, (35)

where p1​[A]p_{1}[A] is the instanton/Pontryagin number of the gauge field AA, defined by

p1​[A]=18​π2​∫M4TrF​u​n​d⁡[FA∧FA].p_{1}[A]=\frac{1}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{M_{4}}\operatorname{Tr}_{Fund}[F_{A}\wedge F_{A}]. (36)

In the case of U⁡(1)U(1), we define p1​[a]=14​π2​∫M4𝑑a∧𝑑ap_{1}[a]=\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}\int_{M_{4}}da\wedge da. Extending the gravitational CS term into the bulk yields the signature term in the bulk action

σ=−124​π2∫M4Trv​e​c[R∧R].\sigma=-\frac{1}{24\pi^{2}}\int_{M_{4}}\operatorname{Tr}_{vec}[R\wedge R]. (37)

With this definition of the parent free Dirac theory coupled to background gauge fields, we can promote aa to be dynamical. It is important however that once thus promoted the bulk action does not depend on aa but only on the remaining background gauge fields. Thus we will first eliminate the dependence of the bulk action above on aa, and express it entirely in terms of the remaining true background gauge fields.

Let us focus on the first two anomaly terms in Eq. (35). Note that if aa was a genuine spinc connection, then p1​[a]/2−σ/8∈ℤp_{1}[a]/2-\sigma/8\in\mathbb{Z}, so that there will be no contribution from that part of the anomaly to the bulk action as

ZD​i​r​a​c∼exp⁡[2​π​i​(3​p1​[a]2−3​σ8)]=1,Z_{Dirac}\sim\exp\left[2\pi i\left(\frac{3p_{1}[a]}{2}-\frac{3\sigma}{8}\right)\right]=1, (38)

independent of the choice of extension into M4M_{4}. However, aa is twisted by the cocycle condition, Eq. (31). Consequently, unless the Brauer class of 𝒜6\mathcal{A}^{6} vanishes,

w2∈H2​(M4,ℤ6)=0,w_{2}\in H^{2}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{6})=0, (39)

p1​[a]/2−σ/8p_{1}[a]/2-\sigma/8 will not be in ℤ\mathbb{Z}. Therefore, as expected the anomaly does not depend on aa and we can hence express the bulk action involving a,𝒜6,g,At​o​pa,\mathcal{A}^{6},g,A_{top} entirely in terms of (𝒜6,g,At​o​p)(\mathcal{A}^{6},g,A_{top}). To that end, let CC be a genuine spinc connection 33 3 Note that every oriented 4-manifold is also a spinc manifold. This guarantees that there always exists such a spinc connection CC. satisfying

∮d​C2​π=∮w2T​M2(mod1).\oint\dfrac{dC}{2\pi}=\oint\frac{w_{2}^{TM}}{2}\pmod{1}. (40)

Then we have B=a−CB=a-C a representative U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field with shifted periods by w2/6w_{2}/6. We can subsequently simplify

p1​[a]=p1​[B+C]=p1​[B]+p1​[C]+2​∫d​C2​π∧d​B2​π.\displaystyle p_{1}[a]=p_{1}[B+C]=p_{1}[B]+p_{1}[C]+2\int\dfrac{dC}{2\pi}\wedge\dfrac{dB}{2\pi}. (41)

Using that

3​(p1​[C]2​π−σ8)∈ℤ,3\left(\dfrac{p_{1}[C]}{2\pi}-\dfrac{\sigma}{8}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}, (42)

we can now simplify the first two terms in Eq. (35) to

Sb​u​l​k2​π​i=32​p1​[B]+3​∫d​C2​π∧d​B2​π+⋯\frac{S_{bulk}}{2\pi i}=\dfrac{3}{2}p_{1}[B]+3\int\dfrac{dC}{2\pi}\wedge\dfrac{dB}{2\pi}+\cdots (43)

Now we simplify the last term in Eq. (35) by writing

∫d​a2​π∧d​𝒜t​o​p2​π\displaystyle\int\frac{da}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi} =∫d​B+d​C2​π∧d​𝒜t​o​p2​π.\displaystyle=\int\frac{dB+dC}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}. (44)

As CC is a spinc connection, we can rewrite

∫d​C2​π∧d​𝒜t​o​p2​π\displaystyle\int\frac{dC}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi} =3​∫d​C2​π∧d​B2​π+∫d​C2​π∧d⁡(𝒜t​o​p−3​B)2​π\displaystyle=3\int\frac{dC}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{dB}{2\pi}+\int\frac{dC}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{d(\mathcal{A}^{top}-3B)}{2\pi} (45)
=3​∫d​C2​π∧d​B2​π+12​(p1​[𝒜t​o​p−3​B+C]−p1​[C])−∫d⁡(𝒜t​o​p−3​B)2​π∧12​d⁡(𝒜t​o​p−3​B)2​π\displaystyle=3\int\frac{dC}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{dB}{2\pi}+\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{top}-3B+C]-p_{1}[C]\right)-\int\frac{d(\mathcal{A}^{top}-3B)}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{1}{2}\frac{d(\mathcal{A}^{top}-3B)}{2\pi} (46)
=3​∫d​C2​π∧d​B2​π−12​∫d⁡(𝒜t​o​p−3​B)2​π∧d⁡(𝒜t​o​p−3​B)2​π\displaystyle=3\int\frac{dC}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{dB}{2\pi}-\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d(\mathcal{A}^{top}-3B)}{2\pi}\wedge\frac{d(\mathcal{A}^{top}-3B)}{2\pi} (47)

Combining the above and substituting into Eq. (35), we obtain

Sb​u​l​k2​π​i=12​p1​[𝒜6]+6​p1​[B]+∫d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∧(12​d​𝒜t​o​p2​π+4⋅d​B2​π).\frac{S_{bulk}}{2\pi i}=\frac{1}{2}p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]+6p_{1}[B]+\int\dfrac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\wedge\left(\frac{1}{2}\dfrac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}+4\cdot\dfrac{dB}{2\pi}\right). (48)

We now observe that

2​d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∧d​B2​π\displaystyle 2\dfrac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\wedge\dfrac{dB}{2\pi} =d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∪w23(mod1),\displaystyle=\dfrac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\cup\frac{w_{2}}{3}\pmod{1}, (49)
6​p1​[B]\displaystyle 6p_{1}[B] =16​𝒫​(w2)(mod1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{6}\mathcal{P}(w_{2})\pmod{1}, (50)

where we have used the Pontryagin square operation [80, 45], 𝒫:H2​(M4,ℤ2​n)→H4​(M4,ℤ4​n)\mathcal{P}\ :\ H^{2}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{2n})\rightarrow H^{4}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{4n}). Therefore, we can obtain the final form of the anomaly

Sb​u​l​k2​π​i=12​p1​[𝒜6]+16​∫𝒫⁡(w2)+∫d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∪(12​d​𝒜t​o​p2​π+2​w23)(mod1).\frac{S_{bulk}}{2\pi i}=\frac{1}{2}p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]+\frac{1}{6}\int\mathcal{P}(w_{2})+\int\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\cup\left(\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}+\frac{2w_{2}}{3}\right)\pmod{1}. (51)

Note that all dependence of the bulk topological action on aa has been eliminated, and thus we can safely promote aa to a dynamical gauge field in the boundary (2+1)​d(2+1)d theory. Eqn. 51 and the subsequent re-expression below (Eqn. 55) are thus the bulk anomaly theory capturing the anomaly of the IR global symmetry of the Nf=6N_{f}=6 QED3 theory.

The first term Eqn. 51 is half of the Pontryagin number of 𝒜6\mathcal{A}^{6}, which is a θ=π\theta=\pi term for the S​U​(6)SU(6) bundle described by 𝒜6\mathcal{A}^{6}. Because 𝒜6\mathcal{A}^{6} is twisted by the center ℤ6\mathbb{Z}_{6} symmetry (or equivalently, it has a nonzero Brauer class w2w_{2}), p1​[𝒜6]p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}] has a fractional part given by 512​∫𝒫⁡(w2)\frac{5}{12}\int\mathcal{P}(w_{2}) [83, 26]. Writing p1​[𝒜6]p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}] as

p1​[𝒜6]=ℐ⁡[𝒜6]+512​∫𝒫⁡(w2),ℐ⁡[𝒜6]∈ℤ,p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]=\mathcal{I}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]+\frac{5}{12}\int\mathcal{P}(w_{2}),\quad\mathcal{I}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]\in\mathbb{Z}, (52)

we do not have a well defined expression for 12​p1​[𝒜6]\frac{1}{2}p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}] purely in terms of the Brauer class w2w_{2}, as 12​p1​[𝒜6]\frac{1}{2}p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}] depends on not only the fractional part of the instanton number, but also the integer part modulo 22. Note that while the relation between instanton number and w2w_{2} holds generally, it can be seen explicitly in the special case where there exists a lift to a U⁡(6)U(6) bundle. Then, we can write

𝒜6=𝒜U⁡(6)−B​𝕀6×6,∮d​B2​π=∮w26(mod1)\mathcal{A}^{6}=\mathcal{A}_{U(6)}-B\mathbb{I}_{6\times 6},\quad\oint\dfrac{dB}{2\pi}=\oint\frac{w_{2}}{6}\pmod{1} (53)

in terms of a U⁡(6)U(6) gauge field 𝒜U⁡(6)\mathcal{A}_{U(6)} under the restriction Tr⁡[𝒜U⁡(6)]=6​B\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal{A}_{U(6)}]=6B. One can then calculate that

p1​[𝒜6]=15​∫d​B2​π∧d​B2​π=512​∫𝒫⁡(w2)(mod1)p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]=15\int\dfrac{dB}{2\pi}\wedge\dfrac{dB}{2\pi}=\dfrac{5}{12}\int\mathcal{P}(w_{2})\pmod{1} (54)

Going back to Eq. (51), we see there is a flavor symmetry anomaly arising from 16​∫𝒫⁡(w2)\frac{1}{6}\int\mathcal{P}(w_{2}). This contribution is nothing more than the fractional part of a θ=−4​π\theta=-4\pi term for the S​U​(6)SU(6) gauge field 𝒜6\mathcal{A}^{6}. Equivalently, one can see −2​p1​[𝒜6]=16​∫𝒫⁡(w2)(mod1)-2p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]=\frac{1}{6}\int\mathcal{P}(w_{2})\pmod{1}, so we can actually rewrite the final form of the anomaly, Eq. (51), as

Sb​u​l​k2​π​i=−32​p1​[𝒜6]+∫d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∪(12​d​𝒜t​o​p2​π+2​w23)(mod1),\displaystyle\frac{S_{bulk}}{2\pi i}=-\frac{3}{2}p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]+\int\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\cup\left(\frac{1}{2}\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}+\frac{2w_{2}}{3}\right)\pmod{1}, (55)

so that the flavor symmetry is completely captured by a θ=−3​π\theta=-3\pi term for the S​U​(6)SU(6) gauge field. We note here the presence of the quotiented ℤ6\mathbb{Z}_{6} center symmetry makes θ\theta periodic under θ∼θ+24​π\theta\sim\theta+24\pi.

The last term in Eq. (55) has a simple interpretation: namely, magnetic particles of U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} transform in a representation of S​U​(6)SU(6) with NN-ality 22 and are fermions. Furthermore, the θ\theta term for U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} ensures that magnetic particles of U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} carry a single electric charge of U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}. Fusing these magnetic particles with the original local monopole, one obtains a particle with zero U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} electric charge, a unit U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} magnetic charge, and 11-ality under S​U​(6)SU(6); this particle can be interpreted to be the remnant of the original Dirac fermion. From another perspective, the bare monopole under 𝒜t​o​p\mathcal{A}^{top} carries charge under the dynamical U⁡(1)U(1) field aa, it can be made local by dressing it with ψ\psi, imparting quantum numbers of ψ\psi to the 𝒜t​o​p{\mathcal{A}}^{top} monopole. We also remark that 12​d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∪d​𝒜t​o​p2​π\frac{1}{2}\frac{d{\mathcal{A}}^{top}}{2\pi}\cup\frac{d{\mathcal{A}}^{top}}{2\pi} is the bulk theory for the nontrivial bosonic topological insulator [74], in which the monopoles are electrically neutral under d​𝒜t​o​pd{\mathcal{A}}^{top} and fermionic, as is reproduced here.

Note that Eq. (55) also describes a time reversal invariant theory. This can be derived from using that 𝒜t​o​p\mathcal{A}^{top} and the original U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field aa (and equivalently, BB) have opposite transformations under time reversal. Then, under time reversal, the first two terms in Eq. (55) change sign, from which we can confirm

𝒯⁡(Sb​u​l​k)−Sb​u​l​k2​π​i\displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{T}(S_{bulk})-S_{bulk}}{2\pi i} =3​p1​[𝒜6]−∫d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∪d​𝒜t​o​p2​π=0(mod1).\displaystyle=3p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]-\int\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\cup\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}=0\pmod{1}. (56)

As desired, the final bulk theory is time reversal invariant on a closed manifold. However, in the presence of a boundary, there are mixed anomalies between time reversal and the flavor symmetry and between time reversal and U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}. This can be seen from analyzing the first two terms in Eq. (55), in which restricting the action on the boundary of an open manifold leads to half quantized Chern Simons terms for both the flavor and U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} gauge fields. On the boundary, time reversal shifts the action by an odd integer Chern Simons term for both the S​U​(6)SU(6) and U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} gauge fields. The anomaly is nontrivial as there is no local counterterm one can add to the original theory to eliminate this shift.

From the nontrivial anomalies, we see that the ultimate fate of Nf=6N_{f}=6 QED3 must be a gapless phase (such as a CFT), a symmetry broken phase, or a symmetry-preserving gapped phase with topological order. For Nf=2N_{f}=2, symmetry-enforced gaplessness is also present, meaning no gapped symmetric topological order can saturate the anomaly. Instead, symmetry breaking is the most likely fate [25] for the IR theory as bootstrap [52] does not support a stable CFT.

For the case of Nf=6N_{f}=6 and the general case of pure QED3 with Nf≥4N_{f}\geq 4, we could not find an analytic argument precluding a gapped, symmetric topologically ordered state in the IR. However, bootstrap studies [20, 51, 4, 31] are consistent with the assumption QED3 with Nf≥4N_{f}\geq 4 realizes a CFT in the IR. Lastly, we remark that there is always an allowed chiral topological order in the IR. As was argued in the previous section, such a state can be realized by the condensation of a chiral mass.

In Appendix F, we describe the anomaly in the case we take the global symmetry to be P​S​U​(3)s×P​S​U​(2)v×U​(1)t​o​pPSU(3)_{s}\times PSU(2)_{v}\times U(1)_{top}, which is relevant as a mid-IR theory of lattice Dirac spin liquids.

IV.2 (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3}

Lastly, we consider including the single symmetry-allowed relevant monopole. Recall the monopole is of the form (Φ1†+Φ2†)∼(f[1†f2†f3]†ℳ†+f[4†f5†f6]†ℳ†)(\Phi_{1}^{\dagger}+\Phi_{2}^{\dagger})\sim(f_{[1}^{\dagger}f_{2}^{\dagger}f_{3]}^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}+f_{[4}^{\dagger}f_{5}^{\dagger}f_{6]}^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}). In this case, we have broken the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} symmetry. However, we have still preserved a (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3} symmetry, where each factor acts as the fundamental on (f1,f2,f3)(f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}) and (f4,f5,f6)(f_{4},f_{5},f_{6}), respectively, and the common center is quotiented out. There are also discrete residual symmetries, including a discrete ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} that acts as swapping f1,2,3,4,5,6→−i​f4,5,6,1,2,3f_{1,2,3,4,5,6}\rightarrow-if_{4,5,6,1,2,3} on the fermions combined with a U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} ℳ†→i​ℳ†\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}\rightarrow i\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}, which acts as Φ1→Φ2\Phi_{1}\rightarrow\Phi_{2} on the monopole. In the UV, this ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} representings the C6C_{6} symmetry swapping the two Dirac valleys.

We will probe the (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3} response by coupling in S​U​(3)SU(3) gauge fields 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}. Note the discrete ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} exchanges 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}. In the UV, 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} represent gauge fields coupling to the two Dirac valleys.

We observe that the separation of the original flavor symmetry into a block diagonal (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3} form constrains the ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} Brauer class of each block to be equal. In other words, defining the classes w2𝒜,w2ℬ∈H2​(M4,ℤ3)w_{2}^{\mathcal{A}},w_{2}^{\mathcal{B}}\in H^{2}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{3}), we have that w2𝒜=w2ℬ≡u2w_{2}^{\mathcal{A}}=w_{2}^{\mathcal{B}}\equiv u_{2}. Therefore, one can equivalently think of (𝒜,ℬ)(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) as two P​S​U​(3)PSU(3) gauge fields that are constrained to have the same obstruction class. We see that upon breaking the P​S​U​(6)→(S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3PSU(6)\rightarrow(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3}, the Brauer class w2∈H2​(M,ℤ6)w_{2}\in H^{2}(M,\mathbb{Z}_{6}) of the parent QED3 is reduced to the diagonal obstruction class u2∈H2​(M,ℤ3)u_{2}\in H^{2}(M,\mathbb{Z}_{3}) by the relationship w2=2​u2(mod6)w_{2}=2u_{2}\pmod{6}.

The anomaly for the theory with the monopole included can be calculated with ease using the result in Eq. (55) found for pure QED3 and breaking the global symmetry accordingly. As the monopole has an expectation value, the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} symmetry is explicitly broken, and hence it is not meaningful to turn on a background gauge field 𝒜t​o​p\mathcal{A}^{top}. Furthermore, the P​S​U​(6)PSU(6) Pontryagin number is changed from p1​[𝒜6]→p1​[𝒜]+p1​[ℬ]p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]\rightarrow p_{1}[\mathcal{A}]+p_{1}[\mathcal{B}]. We then obtain

Sb​u​l​k2​π​i=−32​(p1​[𝒜]+p1​[ℬ]).\frac{S_{bulk}}{2\pi i}=-\frac{3}{2}\left(p_{1}[\mathcal{A}]+p_{1}[\mathcal{B}]\right). (57)

The above represents a θ𝒜,ℬ=−3​π\theta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}=-3\pi term for both S​U​(3)SU(3) gauge fields 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}. Note that under 𝒯I​R{\cal T}_{IR}, both 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} change sign, and thus θ𝒜,ℬ→−θ𝒜,ℬ\theta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}\rightarrow-\theta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}. Because the fractional part of p1​[𝒜]p_{1}[\mathcal{A}] and p1​[ℬ]p_{1}[\mathcal{B}] are both the same, being 13​∫𝒫⁡(w2)\frac{1}{3}\int\mathcal{P}(w_{2}), we see the above is 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR} invariant at any θ\theta a multiple of 3​π3\pi. Similarly since the unitary ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry exchanges 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}, it follows that the anomaly theory is invariant under this symmetry so long as θ𝒜−θℬ=0\theta_{\mathcal{A}}-\theta_{\mathcal{B}}=0 modulo 6​π6\pi. As each of θ𝒜,ℬ\theta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}} is separately 6​π6\pi periodic, it follows that the requirement of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR} invariance constrains θ𝒜=θℬ\theta_{\mathcal{A}}=\theta_{\mathcal{B}} to both either be 00 or to both be 3​π3\pi (modulo 6​π6\pi). The specific theory we have realizes the second possibility where the corresponding boundary theory then has a mixed anomaly between (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3} and 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR}. This implies that the field theory cannot realize a gapped state symmetric under the (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3}, 𝒯I​R{\cal T}_{IR}, and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetries. However, we recall that the UV time reversal 𝒯U​V\mathcal{T}_{UV} actually exchanges the two Dirac valleys. Consequently, we observe there is no mixed anomaly between the IR symmetry and 𝒯U​V\mathcal{T}_{UV}, which is a combination of the discrete ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} exchanging the valleys and the IR time reversal. Instead, 𝒯U​V\mathcal{T}_{UV} constrains θ𝒜,ℬ=−θℬ,𝒜\theta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}=-\theta_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}}, under which the θ\theta angles can flow to be trivial.

Though a trivial symmetry-preserving gapped state is not possible for the boundary theory, we may consider if the IR theory allows a symmetric gapped topological order. We will argue that such a state is not allowed. To see this, can focus on the first S​U​(3)SU(3) factor and break it into its maximal torus, U​(1)2U(1)^{2}. Threading a monopole through its first U⁡(1)U(1) subgroup (with normalization such that the S​U​(3)SU(3) fundamental carries unit electric charge), we see that the anomaly enforces that the monopole has electric charge (1,1/2)(1,1/2). Therefore, for U​(1)2U(1)^{2} charge to be conserved, there must be a quasiparticle in this surface state with these properties. However, the only such particles are those that transform linearly under S​U​(3)SU(3), with integer charges under the U​(1)2U(1)^{2}. Therefore, the hypothetical gapped state cannot saturate the anomaly 44 4 If time reversal symmetry is broken, such as if we allow a chiral mass m​ψ¯​ψm\overline{\psi}\psi, there can be a surface Hall conductivity for the S​U​(3)SU(3). This leads to the monopole threading event to nucleate a (1,1/2)(1,1/2) charge on the surface as required, and there is no obstruction to a gapped symmetry preserving state..

Accordingly, we see the ultimate fate of QED3 perturbed by the allowed monopole must be a symmetry breaking but otherwise trivial phase (where the (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3×ℤ2(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} is broken), an exotic conformal fixed point, or a time reversal broken topologically ordered phase. While the latter two cannot be ruled out, we conjecture that the simplest possible symmetry option, namely, the symmetry broken phase is realized. We will simply assume that this is the case in our subsequent discussion.

IV.3 Unnecessary Criticality

As the anomaly of the DSL with monopole is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} classified, it follows that the anomaly is the same for either sign of λ\lambda. Recall that given the trivial monopole Φt​r​i​v†\Phi^{\dagger}_{triv}, the phase transition is described by

ℒD​S​L+λ(Φt​r​i​v†+h.c.)+⋯,\mathcal{L}_{DSL}+\lambda(\Phi^{\dagger}_{triv}+h.c.)+\cdots, (58)

where ⋯\cdots includes (irrelevant) terms allowed by the microscopic symmetries. We now argue that the DSL is an “unnecessary” quantum critical point, which lies entirely within a single phase [12].

Note that the two signs of λ\lambda are related by an S​U​(6)SU(6) transformation that acts on the Dirac fermions by

U=(01010003×300101003×3100001),ψ→U​ψ.U=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&&&\\ 1&0&0&&0_{3\times 3}&\\ 0&0&1&&&\\ &&&0&1&0\\ &0_{3\times 3}&&1&0&0\\ &&&0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad\psi\rightarrow U\psi. (59)

Thus the ground state of the continuum field theory for λ<0\lambda<0 will be related to the ground state at λ>0\lambda>0 by this S​U​(6)SU(6) transformation.

From the previous section, we accept the conjecture that the RG flow of λ\lambda away from the λ=0\lambda=0 DSL fixed point takes the system to a symmetry broken but otherwise trivial phase. A specific possibility is that the symmetry broken state is just the trimerized VBS ground state of the nearest neighbor spin model in Fig. 2. Microscopically this state preserves the P​S​U​(3)PSU(3), translation, and 𝒯U​V\mathcal{T}_{UV} symmetries but breaks C6C_{6} rotation. In the IR theory, this manifests as a state that breaks the unitary ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} while preserving (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3} (and 𝒯U​V\mathcal{T}_{UV}). The breaking of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} trivializes the anomaly so that there need not be any further topological order or gapless excitations in the resulting ground state. Let us consider the possibility that the flow of λ\lambda lands us in this ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} broken phase.

In terms of the Dirac fermion representation of the continuum Lagrangian, the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry breaking order parameter is ψ¯​μ3​ψ\overline{\psi}\mu^{3}\psi which is invariant under the S​U​(6)SU(6) rotation in Eqn. 59. It follows that if the ground state for λ>0\lambda>0 breaks ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} but is otherwise trivial and gapped, then so will the ground state at λ<0\lambda<0. Then the DSL appears as an unnecessary quantum critical point inside this phase.

Since in the original microscopic system, the trivial ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} broken phase is identified with the VBS phase, we conclude that by tuning one parameter entirely inside this VBS phase, we can reach the DSL as a critical point. Like in other examples of unnecessary criticality, in parameter space, the DSL will live on a surface of codimension one that terminates 55 5 The termination will be described by a multicritical fixed point that we will not attempt to describe here. within the VBS phase so that there is a smooth path that connects either side of this surface.

Alternatively, if instead ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} is preserved but the (S​U​(3)×S​U​(3))/ℤ3(SU(3)\times SU(3))/\mathbb{Z}_{3} symmetry is broken to some subgroup HH in the λ≠0\lambda\neq 0 continuum theory, the S​U​(6)SU(6) rotation that relates λ\lambda to −λ-\lambda will only move us within the corresponding order parameter manifold. The precise “orientation” of the order parameter within this manifold is anyway not fixed by the theory itself, and hence we have the same symmetry breaking pattern for either sign of λ\lambda. Thus once again in the continuum theory we have an unnecssary critical point. In the microscopic system, the corresponding state is an insulator that breaks a UV symmetry such as P​S​U​(3)sPSU(3)_{s} or lattice translation symmetry. Therefore, the DSL can also be an unnecessary critical point within a single S​U​(3)sSU(3)_{s} or translation symmetry breaking phase.

V Discussion and Outlook

In this paper, we studied the possible stability of a DSL in a kagome lattice S​U​(3)SU(3) magnet. Through a careful analysis of the quantum numbers of allowed relevant perturbations at the DSL fixed point, we showed that the DSL is not a stable phase, but instead a quantum critical point, tuned by a symmetry-allowed single-strength monopole.

We performed a detailed analysis of the emergent symmetries and ’t Hooft anomalies of both the critical fixed point as well as the theory obtained in the presence of the relevant perturbation. The presence of anomalies forbid a trivial, symmetric, gapped ground state even when the DSL theory is perturbed away from its critical fixed point. The anomaly of the resulting theory is the same for either sign of the relevant perturbation. The most likely fate is that the RG flow induced by this perturbation leads to a symmetry broken ground state. A specific possibility is a trimer valence bond solid phase that preserves translation and S​U​(3)SU(3) spin symmetries but breaks lattice C6C_{6} rotations. We argued that the DSL is an unnecessary quantum critical point that does not separate two distinct phases but instead lies within a single phase. Thus if the symmetry breaking state is the trimer VBS state, then the DSL is a critical spin liquid living entirely inside this phase and which can be accessed by tuning one parameter. Along with recent results showing the DSL is also an unnecessary quantum critical point on the square lattice antiferromagnet [90], our paper suggests that unnecessary quantum criticality may not be an uncommon phenomenon in quantum many body systems.

It would be insightful for both the study of quantum field theory and spin liquids in real materials to further explore the mechanisms behind quantum critical behavior in QED3 theories. Our work adds to a growing body of literature on the rich behavior of QED3 in lattice systems.

The precise nature of the phase driven by the relevant symmetry-allowed monopole remains an open question, though we presented arguments in favor of a symmetry broken phase. Numerical simulations could help settle this question and to determine the precise pattern of the presumed symmetry breaking.

Lastly, we remark that with recent advances in ultracold atoms experiments, there is hope that the DSL and its neighboring phases could be probed in a laboratory setting. In general, the engineering of S​U​(N)SU(N)-symmetric systems allows for a rich playground on which to explore these exotic quantum phenomena and offers an exciting pathway to probe QED3 in the real world.
