Appendix C Berry phase and Wannier centers

C.1 Berry Phase of Discrete Symmetries

We begin with considering the Berry phase associated with discrete IR symmetries. Note that the overall phase associated with reflection (and charge conjugation, which is not even a lattice symmetry) is not physically meaningful, as it can be changed by a redefinition of the bare monopole operator ℳ→ei​θ​ℳ\mathcal{M}\rightarrow e^{i\theta}\mathcal{M} [72]. While the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} phase associated 𝒞​ℛ\mathcal{CR} is meaningful and has been considered in similar models, it is not relevant here as our underlying kagome lattice model has no 𝒞\mathcal{C} symmetry in the UV at 1/31/3 filling.

Now what remains is time reversal symmetry. Similar to [72], we introduce a Dirac mass ψ¯​μ3​ψ\overline{\psi}\mu^{3}\psi that corresponds to a valley Hall mass. Such a mass does not lead to a nontrivial ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} topological insulator as our spin symmetry is S​U​(3)SU(3) and not S​O​(3)SO(3). Therefore, the monopoles selected by such valley Hall masses should be invariant under the Kramers time reversal i​μ2​𝒯I​Ri\mu^{2}\mathcal{T}_{IR}, which is exactly the lattice time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}. This uniquely fixes the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} phase associated with 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

C.2 Berry Phase of Lattice Symmetries

In order to decompose the band structure of the mean field ansatz, we will use the techinques outlined in [73]. By calculating how rotation acts on the occupied bands at high-symmetry points and comparing it to the spectra of appropriately defined Wannier insulator bands, we can appropriately decompose the spinon bands into a sum (or difference, in the case that fragile topology is present) of Wannier bands. The Wannier bands can be visualized as positive gauge charges sitting at each Wannier center, which contribute to Berry phases upon translation and rotation. In general, a charge qrq_{r} sitting at a rotation center rr leads to the Berry phase under CnC_{n} rotation centered at rr to be

θ⁡(Cn,r)=eqr​2​π​i/n.\theta(C_{n,r})=e^{q_{r}2\pi i/n}. (103)

As mentioned in the main text, it is mandatory we include a quantum valley Hall mass in order to split the spinon bands into Kramers sub-bands with well-defined spectra. We first introduce the mass ψ¯​μ3​ψ\overline{\psi}\mu^{3}\psi (identically for all S​U​(3)SU(3) spins), which favors the monopole Φ1†\Phi^{\dagger}_{1}. In the original unit cell, we will compare the spinon band representation of the Wannier insulator centered on the upward triangle (Γ△\Gamma^{\vartriangle}), centered on the downward triangle (Γ▽\Gamma^{\triangledown}), centered on site (Γ∘\Gamma^{\circ}), and centered on the hexagon (Γ⬡\Gamma^{\varhexagon}). The relevant symmetry operations are the threefold rotations around the upward triangle (C3△C_{3}^{\vartriangle}), downward triangle (C3▽C_{3}^{\triangledown}), and hexagon (C3⬡C_{3}^{\varhexagon}). Note that C6⬡C_{6}^{\varhexagon} is broken down to C3⬡C_{3}^{\varhexagon} by our choice of mass. The high symmetry points are 𝑲\bm{K}, 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime}, and 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}, which are left invariant under C3C_{3}. Note that immediately, simply from the S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetry, we know the Berry phases are trivial. This arises from the fact that the occupied spinon bands Γs​p​i​n​o​n\Gamma^{spinon} must decompose as

Γs​p​i​n​o​n=3⋅(Γ∙+…),\Gamma^{spinon}=3\cdot\left(\Gamma_{\bullet}+\dots\right), (104)

which is a threefold direct sum of a combination of Wannier bands. Therefore, the resulting pattern of gauge charges (in addition to a background −1-1 charge on each site, which is insignificant) centered at each upward triangle, downward triangle, and hexagon will be some number q△,▽,⬡≡0(mod3)q_{\vartriangle,\triangledown,\varhexagon}\equiv 0\pmod{3}, leading to no Berry phase as all of the relevant rotation operation are C3C_{3}. In particular, this means translations T1=(C3▽)−1​C3△T_{1}=(C_{3}^{\triangledown})^{-1}C^{\vartriangle}_{3} and T2=(C3▽)−1​(C△)2​(C3▽)−1T_{2}=(C_{3}^{\triangledown})^{-1}(C^{\vartriangle})^{2}(C_{3}^{\triangledown})^{-1} will also carry no Berry phase. For completeness, we include the explicit results in Table 3.

It still remains to fix is the Berry phase associated with C6C_{6}, which must be ±1\pm 1 from our above analysis. To isolate the C6C_{6} action, we could introduce a mass −ψ¯​μ1​ψ-\overline{\psi}\mu^{1}\psi, which favors the monopole Φ1†+Φ2†+Φ3†+Φ4†\Phi^{\dagger}_{1}+\Phi^{\dagger}_{2}+\Phi^{\dagger}_{3}+\Phi^{\dagger}_{4}. Introducing ψ¯​μ1​ψ\overline{\psi}\mu^{1}\psi breaks down T1,2T_{1,2} into (T1+T2,2​T2−T1)(T_{1}+T_{2},2T_{2}-T_{1}), tripling the spatial unit cell while preserving the original hexagon-centered C6C_{6}. We must focus on the rotation action centered on the hexagonal sites the corner of the unit cell, as those are the only symmetries of our spinon bands. However, repeating our previous analysis at the high symmetry point Γ\Gamma does not uniquely constrain the C6C_{6} Berry phase because multiple Wannier patterns could give rise to the same symmetry representation.

Instead, we can find the Berry phase numerically. In order to do this, we place the spin liquid on a finite torus with 2​π2\pi flux uniformly spread. We can then find that the monopoles with definite C6C_{6} angular momentum, Φ1†±Φ2†\Phi_{1}^{\dagger}\pm\Phi_{2}^{\dagger}, transform under C6C_{6} with eigenvalues ±1\pm 1. Note that using a remaining phase ambiguity of the monopoles, we have fixed the relative phase between Φ1†\Phi_{1}^{\dagger} and Φ2†\Phi_{2}^{\dagger} such that C6​(Φ1†)=Φ2†C_{6}(\Phi_{1}^{\dagger})=\Phi_{2}^{\dagger}, and both phase choices do not affect the existence of the single nontrivial monopole.

Appendix D Comments on Monopole-Antimonopole Pairs

In this appendix, we analyze the relevance of other operators in the zero flux sector, generated by single monopole-antimonopole pairs Φ†​Φ\Phi^{\dagger}\Phi, to argue that the DSL is a quantum critical point. In order for the DSL to be an un-fine tuned quantum critical point, these operators must all be irrelevant if they are invariant under all microscopic symmetries. To begin, the all single monopole-antimonopole pairs are charge neutral under U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}, so we will label the operators by their global S​U​(6)SU(6) representation. As Φ\Phi and Φ†\Phi^{\dagger} transform in the 𝟐𝟎\mathbf{20} representation of S​U​(6)SU(6), Φ†​Φ\Phi^{\dagger}\Phi transforms as

𝟐𝟎⊗𝟐𝟎=𝟏⊕𝟑𝟓⊕𝟏𝟕𝟓⊕𝟏𝟖𝟗\mathbf{20}\otimes\mathbf{20}=\mathbf{1}\oplus\mathbf{35}\oplus\mathbf{175}\oplus\mathbf{189} (110)

The singlet 𝟏\mathbf{1} corresponds to a four fermion term. The most relevant operator in this channel is chiral and not symmetry allowed, while the next most relevant operator in this channel is symmetryt allowed but likely irrelevant, with scaling dimension ∼4.35\sim 4.35 from large NfN_{f} [19]. The 𝟑𝟓\mathbf{35} transforms like the adjoint and is therefore not symmetry allowed. Lastly, there are allowed terms in the 𝟏𝟕𝟓\mathbf{175} and 𝟏𝟖𝟗\mathbf{189} channels, but both of these operators are likely irrelevant, with scaling dimensions approximately 4.414.41 and 3.843.84, respectively from large NfN_{f} [19]. Note that there are operators in the 𝟏𝟖𝟗\mathbf{189} corresponding to four-fermion operators that have scaling dimension ∼2.92\sim 2.92 from large NfN_{f}. In general, these may be UV allowed, so we must assume that they are irrelevant in order for the DSL to be a true critical point. The assumptions we make here are similar to the ones made in in order for there to be a stable Nf=4N_{f}=4 DSL on the triangular and kagome lattices [31], and a DSL critical point on the square lattice [90].

Appendix E The Kagome Lattice Chiral Spin Liquid

In this appendix, we consider the condensation of a chiral (quantum Hall) mass ψ¯​ψ\overline{\psi}{\psi}, which breaks time reversal and reflection symmetry, generating an intermediate chiral spin liquid (CSL) phase at intermediate UU. We remark that while a CSL is found on the kagome lattice for the Heisenberg coupling with chiral ring-exchange terms [85, 86], one could imagine such a chiral state emerging through the spontaneous breaking of time reversal and reflection. The CSL hosts topological order, anyon excitations, and gapless edge states. Moreover, the induced Chern-Simons term from the singlet mass suppresses monopole proliferation as the monopoles will become electrically charged and linearly confined [58, 1]. After integrating out the gapped fermions, the specific topological order generated in this case is described by the KK-matrix

KC​S​L=(2112),K_{CSL}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\ 1&2\end{pmatrix}, (111)

identical to that of the Halperin (221)(221) quantum Hall state [85], with three superselection sectors spanned by an anyon aa such that a3=1a^{3}=1 and θa=2​π/3\theta_{a}=2\pi/3. The edge theory contains two copropagating bosonic modes and is captured by the S​U​(3)1SU(3)_{1} chiral Wess-Zumino-Witten CFT.

Appendix F P​S​U​(3)s×P​S​U​(2)v×U​(1)t​o​pPSU(3)_{s}\times PSU(2)_{v}\times U(1)_{top} Anomaly

It is also insightful to consider the anomaly when we break S​U​(6)→S​U​(3)s×S​U​(2)vSU(6)\rightarrow SU(3)_{s}\times SU(2)_{v}. Such a branching pattern is applicable as the action of the UV spin and lattice/valley symmetries often decouple exactly this way when embedded into the IR, including for our kagome lattice ansatz and many other parton models. Therefore, this can be considered as the effective global symmetry in a mid-IR regime. We will proceed exactly as in the main text, coupling the QED3 to S​U​(3)sSU(3)_{s} gauge field 𝒜s\mathcal{A}^{s}, S​U​(2)vSU(2)_{v} gauge field 𝒜v\mathcal{A}^{v}, and a U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} gauge field 𝒜t​o​p\mathcal{A}^{top}. As before, the dynamical U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field coupled to the Dirac fermions is denoted by aa. Defining the classes w2s∈H2​(M4,ℤ3)w_{2}^{s}\in H^{2}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{3}), w2v∈H2​(M4,ℤ2)w_{2}^{v}\in H^{2}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{2}), and w2T​M∈H2​(M4,ℤ2)w_{2}^{TM}\in H^{2}(M_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{2}) as the Brauer and Stiefel-Whitney classes of the S​U​(3)sSU(3)_{s}, S​U​(2)vSU(2)_{v}, and tangent bundles respectively, we have the cocyle compatibility condition

∮d​a2​π+13​w2s+12​w2v+12​w2T​M∈ℤ.\oint\frac{da}{2\pi}+\frac{1}{3}w_{2}^{s}+\frac{1}{2}w_{2}^{v}+\frac{1}{2}w_{2}^{TM}\in\mathbb{Z}. (112)

The cocycle condition restricts fields with charge 11 under U⁡(1)U(1) to be fermionic and transform in the fundamentals of the corresponding spin and valley symmetry groups. The presence of w2vw_{2}^{v} also leads to a fractional quantization of the flux

∮12​w2v+d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∈ℤ.\oint\frac{1}{2}w_{2}^{v}+\frac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\in\mathbb{Z}. (113)

To calculate the ’t Hooft anomaly, one can go through the full calculation as in the pure QED3 case or take Eq. (55) and use the symmetry breaking pattern to decompose p1​[𝒜6]=3​p1​[𝒜v]+2​p1​[𝒜v]p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{6}]=3p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{v}]+2p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{v}]. In both cases, we obtain

Sb​u​l​k2​π​i\displaystyle\frac{S_{bulk}}{2\pi i} =−12​p1​[𝒜v]+∫d​𝒜t​o​p2​π∧(12​d​𝒜t​o​p2​π+w2s3)(mod1).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}p_{1}[\mathcal{A}^{v}]+\int\dfrac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}\wedge\left(\frac{1}{2}\dfrac{d\mathcal{A}^{top}}{2\pi}+\frac{w_{2}^{s}}{3}\right)\pmod{1}. (114)

Notably, in Eq. (114) there is the absence of a term ∼w2s∪w2v\sim w_{2}^{s}\cup w_{2}^{v}, which would indicate a mixed anomaly between valley and spin flavor symmetries. This is is a generalization of the parity anomaly of Dirac fermions, and while it would be present in cases Nf=0(mod4)N_{f}=0\pmod{4}, we see it is absent here. Instead, there is only an anomaly for the S​U​(2)vSU(2)_{v} symmetry. Therefore, we expect that without the monopole state, the Dirac spin liquid should still be able to realize a gapped state with full S​U​(3)sSU(3)_{s} spin symmetry. As before one can still see the full bulk action is time reversal invariant, although there is still mixed time reversal anomalies with the flavor and flux conservation symmetries.

The final term in Eq. (114) contains the anomalies involving U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}. Specifically, using similar arguments as from the main text, one can see that the magnetic particles of U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} are still the Dirac fermions, which transform in the S​U​(3)sSU(3)_{s} and S​U​(2)vSU(2)_{v} fundamentals.

Quite generally for pure QED3, we see that even after decomposing the S​U​(Nf)SU(N_{f}) flavor symmetry into a tensor product symmetry group as is common in parton constructions and lattice models, the key aspects of the QED3 anomaly structure are still present.
